rules.title: Web Server Webshell Upload and Access Attempt
rules.description: Correlates an nginx access-log webshell upload (POST to an upload-like path, executable/double-extension filename such as shell.php.jpg, small or unknown response size, 200/201) with a same-clientip GET to the identical URL within 15 minutes -- an upload alone is routine web traffic, pairing it with the follow-up activation attempt is the actual signal. Sigma's detection: block cannot express a cross-event, time-windowed join (no correlation: rule type in this repo's schema -- checked docs/schemas/sigma_schema.json), so the real logic lives in custom.splunk.raw_query, the same escape hatch DETECT-2026-0002/0003 use for their own correlations (those use streamstats time_window threshold-counting on one event type; this rule needs a two-event pairing instead). Uses a streamstats carry-forward join: eval a marker to null() on non-matching rows, then `streamstats current=f last(eval(...))` per clientip+uri_path carries the most recent prior upload's _time onto every later row in that group, so a GET within 900s of the carried value is the pairing -- same streamstats family and "raw_query is the fallback, not one fixed SPL shape" precedent as 0002/0003, just the carry-forward variant instead of threshold-counting. The schedule is coupled to that 900s gap instead of copying the rest of the nginx family's -5m/*/5: a scheduled search only sees a pair whose two events both fall inside one window, so earliest has to be at least (cron interval + the correlation gap). -30m with */15 is the minimum-overlap (2x) form of that guarantee; -30m/*/5 satisfied it too but re-evaluated every pair on six consecutive runs. Some residual duplication is inherent -- non-overlapping windows would drop every pair straddling a run boundary, and custom.splunk has no suppress/throttle field for Splunk-side alert throttling -- so the raw_query ends with `| dedup clientip uri_path`, collapsing repeat activation GETs of the same shell within a run. Replaces an earlier transaction/closed_txn draft: functionally equivalent (confirmed in Bjorn's prior review) but transaction is Splunk's own documented scale anti-pattern (single- threaded, doesn't distribute like stats-family commands) and had zero other precedent in this repo. The detection: block below is a schema-required placeholder covering only the upload half and is never evaluated. Ported from NetWitness ESA-066's `FROM PATTERN ... timer:within(15 Min)` rule (same 15-minute window, same extension/path/size gates); the extension list and double-extension evasion form were cross-checked against current file-upload-bypass write-ups. Three scope limits are documented in falsepositives rather than papered over: the pairing needs the POST and the later GET to carry an identical uri_path, the upload-directory gate accepts only uploads?/files?/file-manager/tmp (so /media/, /assets/, /images/ and theme folders are out of pattern), and trailing-dot/ null-byte extension variants are not matched. No SigmaHQ/Splunk/ Elastic rule covers this exact upload-then-access pairing; SigmaHQ's windows webshell-strings rule and Splunk's CVE-specific webshell-access analytics are single-event and were used only to sanity-check the extension/path vocabulary, not the correlation shape. Tagged T1505.003 only -- an access-log line only shows the attempted upload and reactivation, never that the uploaded file actually executed anything.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: A legitimate upload feature whose stored filename happens to end in an executable extension (rare, but .cgi/.pl still back some form handlers) followed by the client's own confirmation GET of the file it just uploaded -- a common upload-widget UX pattern.
Your own scanner or upload fuzzer (Burp Intruder, ffuf --data, upload-bypass tooling) replaying an upload+GET pair against a test endpoint -- correlate with the scan calendar before escalating.

Known blind spots, documented rather than fixed -- these are scope limits of the pairing, not logic errors. (a) The join keys on `clientip` AND an identical `uri_path`, so the POST and the follow-up GET must address the exact same URL: an upload that answers 302 and hands back a different (rewritten, hashed or CDN-fronted) retrieval URL never pairs. (b) is_upload_dir only accepts uploads?/files?/file-manager/tmp directories, so a shell dropped into /media/, /assets/, /images/ or a CMS theme folder is out of pattern even when the POST and GET URLs do match. (c) The extension regex covers the double-extension evasion form (shell.php.jpg) but not the trailing-dot (shell.php.) or null-byte (shell.php%00.jpg) variants. Any of the three means no alert at all, not a late one.
rules.rule_body: index=main sourcetype=access_combined | eval uri_path_lc=lower(uri_path) | eval is_exec_ext=if(match(uri_path_lc, "\.(php[3457]?|phtml|phar|pht|asp|aspx|jsp|jspx|jspa|cgi|py|sh|rb|cfm|shtml)(\..+)?$"), 1, 0) | eval is_upload_dir=if(match(uri_path_lc, "(^|/)(uploads?|files?|file-manager|tmp)(/|$)"), 1, 0) | eval is_upload_event=if(method="POST" AND is_exec_ext=1 AND is_upload_dir=1 AND (status="200" OR status="201") AND (isnull(bytes) OR bytes<5000), 1, 0) | eval is_access_event=if(method="GET" AND is_exec_ext=1, 1, 0) | where is_upload_event=1 OR is_access_event=1 | sort 0 _time | streamstats current=f last(eval(if(is_upload_event=1, _time, null()))) as last_upload_time by clientip uri_path | where is_access_event=1 AND isnotnull(last_upload_time) AND (_time - last_upload_time) <= 900 | eval duration=_time - last_upload_time | dedup clientip uri_path | table _time, host, clientip, method, uri_path, uri_query, status, bytes, useragent, referer, duration

rules.title: Web Server Webshell Command Execution via Query String
rules.description: Detects nginx access-log GET requests with HTTP 200 whose query string carries a Linux post-exploitation command artifact -- a likely already-placed webshell being driven through its command parameter (e.g. ?x=whoami, ?f=wget%20..., ?cmd=;id). Linux-only and GET+200-only by design, matching the scope of the NetWitness source this is ported from (ESA-072): a webshell's exact interface and HTTP verb vary too much to generalize further from an access log alone. Covers three shapes: (1) a bare command/binary name as a parameter value, with space in its `+`/%20/double-encoded %2520 forms and a mandatory terminator so the name has to be the whole value rather than its prefix; (2) cmd=/exec=/command= gated on a confirmatory shell metacharacter or a token-anchored known binary in the value, not the parameter name alone -- the same FP lesson the source rule already learned in production (bare `id` stays excluded entirely, since `?id=` is an ordinary cache-busting param); (3) direct code-exec/reverse-shell indicators (eval(, system(, /dev/tcp/, /etc/passwd) that need no confirmation. Both confirmatory shapes were tightened 2026-09-26 after review found two systematic FP classes: `&`/`%26` had been listed as confirmatory "shell metacharacters" in (2) even though in a query string they are the parameter separator (so cmd=view&page=2 confirmed itself), and the binary names in both (1) and (2) were unanchored substrings that fired on cmd=publish/cmd=dashboard ("sh"), cmd=finance ("nc"), cmd=catalog ("cat"), auth=sshkey, pkg=perlbrew and url=curl.se. Both shapes now require the binary name to be a whole token; `&` survives only as a right-hand terminator, which is the value ending rather than evidence of a shell. Cross-checked against SigmaHQ's web_win_webshells_in_access_logs.yml (same shape -- =whoami/=cmd style GET params -- but Windows-command flavored; this rule is the Linux-command counterpart Masha's nginx gap analysis flagged as missing). Single-event pattern, expressed as a normal Sigma detection: block (no correlation needed, unlike DETECT-2026-0039). Known blind spots, same as the source: POST-body command execution (e.g. China Chopper) and base64/obfuscated/ string-concatenated commands are invisible to a static keyword/regex match on the query string.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: A wiki/docs page whose query string legitimately contains an OS command name (e.g. a search for "whoami" or a Linux tutorial URL) -- the source rule's own production tuning found this rare enough to accept, since the alternative (dropping bare command names entirely) misses the most common real webshell interaction shape.

An app that genuinely uses cmd=/exec=/command= as a parameter name for a non-shell purpose (e.g. cmd=view, cmd=export) -- excluded unless the value also carries a shell metacharacter or a whole-token binary name, per the two confirmatory branches in selection_cmd_param. Values that merely *contain* a binary name (cmd=publish, cmd=dashboard, cmd=finance, cmd=catalog) and values simply followed by another parameter (cmd=view&page=2) no longer confirm.

A parameter whose entire value legitimately equals a command name still matches selection_cmd_keyword -- lang=python is the realistic example, and it is indistinguishable from ?x=python at the access-log level. Accepted for the same reason as the wiki/docs case above: dropping bare command names would cost the most common real webshell interaction shape. Prefix collisions (auth=sshkey, pkg=perlbrew, url=curl.se, q=telnetd) are excluded by the mandatory terminator.
rules.rule_body:
detection:
  selection_sourcetype:
    sourcetype: access_combined
  selection_method:
    method: GET
  selection_status:
    status: '200'
  selection_cmd_keyword:
    uri_query|re: (?i)=(?:whoami|uname|wget|curl|python3?|perl|ruby|ssh|ncat|socat|telnet|chmod|mkfifo)(?:\+|%20|%2520|&|%26|;|%3b|$)
  selection_cmd_keyword_flag:
    uri_query|re: (?i)(?:php(?:\+|%20|%2520)-r|nc(?:\+|%20|%2520)-|bash(?:\+|%20|%2520)-i|sh(?:\+|%20|%2520)-c|cat(?:\+|%20|%2520)/etc/|base64(?:\+|%20|%2520)-d|openssl(?:\+|%20|%2520)s_client)
  selection_cmd_param:
    uri_query|re: (?i)(?:cmd|exec|command)=(?:[a-z0-9_\-%./]*(?:;|\||`|\$\(|%3b|%7c|%60|%24%28)|(?:[a-z0-9_\-%./]*[^a-z0-9])?(?:whoami|uname|wget|curl|python3?|perl|ruby|ssh|ncat|socat|telnet|nc|bash|sh|cat|base64|chmod|mkfifo|openssl)(?:\+|%20|%2520|&|%26|;|%3b|\||%7c|/|$))
  selection_direct_indicator:
    uri_query|contains:
    - eval(
    - system(
    - /dev/tcp/
    - /etc/passwd
  condition: "selection_sourcetype and selection_method and selection_status and (\n  selection_cmd_keyword\
    \ or selection_cmd_keyword_flag or\n  selection_cmd_param or selection_direct_indicator\n)\n"

rules.title: Web Server SQL Injection Attempt in Request Path or Query
rules.description: Detects nginx access-log GET/POST requests on any status except 404 whose request path or query string carries one of nine SQLi shapes: UNION-based, quoted-tautology bypass ('OR'1'='1), comment-based termination after a quote (--/#), boolean-blind (AND/OR + numeric compare), time-blind (SLEEP/BENCHMARK/WAITFOR DELAY/PG_SLEEP/ DBMS_PIPE.RECEIVE_MESSAGE), error-based (EXTRACTVALUE/UPDATEXML/ FLOOR(RAND(/EXP(~), schema/version recon (information_schema, @@version, DATABASE()), stacked queries (;DROP/INSERT/...) and payload-builder functions (CONCAT/GROUP_CONCAT/hex literals/CHAR()). Ported from NetWitness ESA-067 (same nine categories, same FP gates: boolean-blind requires the numeric-compare pair together, not a bare and/or; tautology/comment require an actual quote character present). Cross-checked against SigmaHQ's web_sql_injection_in_access_logs.yml, which independently covers the same core keyword set (UNION SELECT, information_schema, sleep(10), '1'='1) -- confirms the category list rather than replacing it, and that rule's own note that WAF-bypass research now also documents comment-based whitespace substitution (/**/ in place of a literal space) and JSON-body SQLi that this access-log-only view cannot see (see falsepositives/limits). Checks both uri_path and uri_query, unlike the SigmaHQ rule (GET query only) and the NetWitness source (single combined url field) -- a payload that trips a 400 before reaching the app is logged in uri_path, not uri_query. Attempt-only signal (T1190): the access log has no response body, so a 500 here means the server errored, not that data was extracted. Status handling matches SigmaHQ's rule: 404 is excluded and nothing else is. An earlier 200/201/500 allow-list was replaced 2026-09-26 because it contradicted the uri_path half of this same rule -- the reason uri_path is checked at all is that nginx rejects a traversal-ish or malformed payload with a 400 before the application sees it, and an allow-list that omits 400 discards exactly those requests -- and because it also dropped the 403/302 answers scanners routinely collect, at no gain in precision: the nine payload patterns, not the response code, are what make this rule specific.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: A scanner you run yourself (sqlmap, Burp, an internal ASV scan) sends exactly these payloads by design -- correlate with the scan calendar or source IP before escalating; no allow-list built in, since one keyed on host/IP would also hide a genuine probe.
selection_recon's `database()`/`version()` and selection_stacked's keyword list can appear in a legitimate app's own query-string tokens (rare, but not impossible on a CMS with verbose URLs).

Known blind spot inherited from the source rule: POST-body payloads are invisible in the access log, comment-based whitespace obfuscation (/**/-as-space) is only partly covered (only inside selection_union's own pattern), and JSON-body SQLi (increasingly reported bypassing WAFs in 2025-2026) is not visible here at all.

selection_payload_builder's `0x[0-9a-f]{10,}` hex-literal pattern matches any long lowercase-hex token in the URL, whatever its purpose: token=0xa1b2c3d4e5f6a7, hash=0x12345678901234 and similar session IDs, cache-busting values, content digests and crypto addresses all trip it with no SQL anywhere in the request. This is the most likely application-driven FP in the whole rule -- unlike the other eight categories it needs no SQL keyword, quote or comment marker to fire, only a hex string long enough. Check this pattern first if the rule is noisy against a specific app.

Alert volume, not false positives: SQLi probing is constant background radiation on any internet-facing host. Treat as an activity/enrichment signal; only 404 is filtered, so the status field in the output is what separates a rejected attempt (400) or blocked one (403) from an answered 200 and from an error-based 500.
rules.rule_body:
detection:
  selection_sourcetype:
    sourcetype: access_combined
  selection_method:
    method:
    - GET
    - POST
  filter_notfound:
    status: '404'
  selection_union:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)union(?:\+|%20|/\*.*?\*/)*(?:all(?:\+|%20)*)?select
  - uri_query|re: (?i)union(?:\+|%20|/\*.*?\*/)*(?:all(?:\+|%20)*)?select
  selection_tautology:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:or|and)(?:\+|%20)*(?:%27|\x27)?[a-z0-9_]+(?:%27|\x27)?(?:\+|%20)*(?:=|%3d)(?:\+|%20)*(?:%27|\x27)?[a-z0-9_]+(?:%27|\x27)?
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:or|and)(?:\+|%20)*(?:%27|\x27)?[a-z0-9_]+(?:%27|\x27)?(?:\+|%20)*(?:=|%3d)(?:\+|%20)*(?:%27|\x27)?[a-z0-9_]+(?:%27|\x27)?
  selection_comment:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:--|%2d%2d|#|%23)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:--|%2d%2d|#|%23)
  selection_boolean_blind:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)\b(?:and|or)\b(?:\+|%20)+\(?[0-9]+(?:=|%3d|<|>)\(?[a-z0-9_]+
  - uri_query|re: (?i)\b(?:and|or)\b(?:\+|%20)+\(?[0-9]+(?:=|%3d|<|>)\(?[a-z0-9_]+
  selection_time_blind:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:sleep\(|benchmark\(|waitfor(?:\+|%20)delay|pg_sleep\(|dbms_pipe\.receive_message)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:sleep\(|benchmark\(|waitfor(?:\+|%20)delay|pg_sleep\(|dbms_pipe\.receive_message)
  selection_error_based:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:extractvalue\(|updatexml\(|floor\(rand\(|exp\(~)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:extractvalue\(|updatexml\(|floor\(rand\(|exp\(~)
  selection_recon:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:information_schema|sysobjects|syscolumns|sys\.tables|@@version|@@datadir|version\(\)|database\(\))
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:information_schema|sysobjects|syscolumns|sys\.tables|@@version|@@datadir|version\(\)|database\(\))
  selection_stacked:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:;|%3b)(?:\+|%20)*(?:drop|insert|update|delete|exec|create|alter)(?:\+|%20)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:;|%3b)(?:\+|%20)*(?:drop|insert|update|delete|exec|create|alter)(?:\+|%20)
  selection_payload_builder:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:concat\(.{0,60}?,|group_concat\(|0x[0-9a-f]{10,}|char\(\s*0x?[0-9]+\s*(?:,|\)))
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:concat\(.{0,60}?,|group_concat\(|0x[0-9a-f]{10,}|char\(\s*0x?[0-9]+\s*(?:,|\)))
  condition: "selection_sourcetype and selection_method and (\n  selection_union or selection_tautology\
    \ or selection_comment or\n  selection_boolean_blind or selection_time_blind or\n  selection_error_based\
    \ or selection_recon or selection_stacked or\n  selection_payload_builder\n) and not filter_notfound\n"

rules.title: Web Server Cross-Site Scripting Attempt in Request Path or Query
rules.description: Detects nginx access-log GET/POST requests on any status except 404 whose request path or query string carries one of nine reflected-XSS shapes: script-tag injection (<script), event-handler injection (onerror=/ onload=/onclick= etc.), javascript: URI scheme, dangerous HTML tags (<img/<svg/<iframe/<body/<input/<video/<audio/<marquee), DOM-exfil references (document.cookie, window.location), JS-exec/obfuscation calls (eval(/atob(/String.fromCharCode(), PoC alert functions (alert(/ confirm(/prompt(), attribute/tag-breakout (a quote then > then a new <), and HTML-entity-encoded script tags (<script, <script, <script). Ported from NetWitness ESA-068 (same nine categories and the same two FP gates: the dangerous-tag pattern requires the opening `<`/%3c directly before the tag name, and the JS-exec/PoC-function patterns require the opening parenthesis). Cross-checked against SigmaHQ's web_xss_in_access_logs.yml, which independently covers the same core set (<script>, <iframe, <svg, document.cookie/domain, onerror=/onload=, javascript:alert) -- confirms the category list rather than replacing it. Reflected-XSS-only, same as both source rules: the access log has no response body (reflection can't be confirmed, only the attempt) and no request body (POST-borne or DOM-based/client-side-only XSS, now the dominant shape on React/Vue/Angular SPAs per current WAF-bypass research, is invisible here). Checks both uri_path and uri_query, unlike the SigmaHQ rule (query only) and the NetWitness source (single combined url field). Status handling matches SigmaHQ's rule: 404 is excluded and nothing else is. An earlier 200/201 allow-list was replaced 2026-09-26 because it contradicted the uri_path half of this same rule -- the reason uri_path is checked at all is that nginx answers a malformed payload with a 400 before the application sees it, and an allow-list that omits 400 discards exactly those requests -- and because it dropped the 403/302 answers scanners routinely collect at no gain in precision. Tagged T1189 (Drive-by Compromise), not T1190: ATT&CK's own T1189 page names cross-site scripting as a delivery form ("Built-in web application interfaces that allow user-controllable content are leveraged for the insertion of malicious scripts or iFrames (e.g., cross-site scripting)") and draws the boundary at whose software is exploited -- T1189 targets a client endpoint on visiting the page, T1190 targets the server-side application. Reflected XSS lands squarely on the client-side side of that line, which is also why SigmaHQ's own web_xss_in_access_logs.yml carries attack.t1189 while its sibling SQLi rule carries attack.t1190. The sibling rules here (DETECT-2026-0041 SQLi, 0037 traversal, 0043 Log4Shell) keep T1190 because those payloads do exploit the server.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: A scanner you run yourself (XSStrike, dalfox, an internal ASV scan) sends exactly these payloads by design -- correlate with the scan calendar or source IP before escalating; no allow-list built in, since one keyed on host/IP would also hide a genuine probe.
A page that legitimately embeds `<video`/`<audio`/`<iframe` markup or `document.cookie`/`alert(` text in a query parameter (e.g. a rich-text/preview or a "share this code snippet" feature).

Known blind spot inherited from both source rules: POST-body and DOM-based (client-side-only, never reaching the server in the URL) XSS are invisible here; current WAF-bypass research documents parameter-pollution XSS specifically evading URL-pattern detection like this one.

Alert volume, not false positives: XSS probing is constant background radiation on any internet-facing host, same as the SQLi/traversal rules. Treat as an activity/enrichment signal; only 404 is filtered, so the status field in the output is what separates a rejected attempt (400) or blocked one (403) from an answered 200.
rules.rule_body:
detection:
  selection_sourcetype:
    sourcetype: access_combined
  selection_method:
    method:
    - GET
    - POST
  filter_notfound:
    status: '404'
  selection_script_tag:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:<|%3c)(?:\+|%20)*script
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:<|%3c)(?:\+|%20)*script
  selection_event_handler:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)\bon(?:error|load|mouseover|mouseout|focus|blur|click|change|submit)(?:\+|%20)*(?:=|%3d)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)\bon(?:error|load|mouseover|mouseout|focus|blur|click|change|submit)(?:\+|%20)*(?:=|%3d)
  selection_js_uri:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)javascript(?::|%3a)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)javascript(?::|%3a)
  selection_dangerous_tag:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:<|%3c)(?:\+|%20)*(?:img|svg|iframe|body|input|video|audio|marquee)\b
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:<|%3c)(?:\+|%20)*(?:img|svg|iframe|body|input|video|audio|marquee)\b
  selection_dom_exfil:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:document\.(?:cookie|write|location|domain)|window\.location)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:document\.(?:cookie|write|location|domain)|window\.location)
  selection_js_exec:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:eval\(|atob\(|unescape\(|decodeuricomponent\(|string\.fromcharcode\(|settimeout\(|setinterval\()
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:eval\(|atob\(|unescape\(|decodeuricomponent\(|string\.fromcharcode\(|settimeout\(|setinterval\()
  selection_poc_alert:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)\b(?:alert|confirm|prompt)\(
  - uri_query|re: (?i)\b(?:alert|confirm|prompt)\(
  selection_attr_breakout:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:%22|\x22|%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:>|%3e)(?:<|%3c)
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:%22|\x22|%27|\x27)(?:\+|%20)*(?:>|%3e)(?:<|%3c)
  selection_entity_encoded:
  - uri_path|re: (?i)(?:&|%26)(?:lt|#0*60|#x0*3c);?.{0,10}script
  - uri_query|re: (?i)(?:&|%26)(?:lt|#0*60|#x0*3c);?.{0,10}script
  condition: "selection_sourcetype and selection_method and (\n  selection_script_tag or selection_event_handler\
    \ or\n  selection_js_uri or selection_dangerous_tag or selection_dom_exfil or\n  selection_js_exec\
    \ or selection_poc_alert or selection_attr_breakout or\n  selection_entity_encoded\n) and not filter_notfound\n"

rules.title: Web Server Log4Shell JNDI Injection Attempt in Request Path, Query, or Headers
rules.description: Detects the `${jndi:...}` lookup syntax used to exploit Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) and its known obfuscation forms across four nginx access-log fields: useragent, referer, uri_path and uri_query -- the same fields the earliest 2021 attacks abused (User-Agent and X-Api-Version headers were the original delivery vector, quickly followed by any reflected/logged request field) and the ones this repo's own web rules already check (0037/0040/0041/0042 all check uri_path+uri_query, 0038 checks useragent). X-Api-Version itself -- and every other custom or proxy header the 2021 wave abused (X-Forwarded-For, Authorization, Cookie) -- is a documented blind spot rather than a covered field: this repo's nginx log_format captures only the request line, User-Agent and Referer, so there is no field for the rule to check. Recovering it is an nginx log_format change, not a pattern change; see falsepositives. Ported from SigmaHQ's web_cve_2021_44228_log4j.yml: four selection groups mirror its 23-entry keyword list -- direct `${jndi:<scheme>:/` lookups (ldap/rmi/ldaps/dns/ nis/nds/corba/iiop), percent- and double/triple-encoded markers, nested `${}` substitution/default-value bypass tricks that spell out "jndi"/"ldap" without the literal substring, and a base64-wrapped variant -- `${base64:JHtqbmRp`, where the magic prefix JHtqbmRp is simply the base64 encoding of `${jndi`, a documented WAF-bypass form. The source rule's `Reference Class Name: foo` entry is excluded: that string is log4j's own server-side exception output, not something a client ever supplies in a request field this access log captures, so it cannot appear in useragent/referer/uri_path/uri_query. The source rule's Nessus filter (its own safe validation payload, w.nessus.org/nessus or /nessus}) is kept as an explicit `not filter_nessus` exclusion rather than silently dropped -- deliberately the opposite treatment to DETECT-2026-0038, which matches "Nessus" as a scanner User-Agent on purpose; see falsepositives for why that split is intentional. Continued relevance per a 2026 network-telescope study (Dec 2021-Oct 2025): generic obfuscated JNDI probes are still high-volume background scanning years post-disclosure (GreyNoise currently tracks 100+ active scanning nodes), so this is cheap, high-specificity coverage for a gap none of the other seven web rules fill. web_jndi_exploit.yml (JNDI-Exploit-Kit paths like /Basic/ReverseShell/) was deliberately left out: those paths are the attacker's own LDAP/HTTP callback server's served-payload paths, but a real delivery still carries them inside the initial `${jndi:ldap://.../ Basic/...}` URI, which selection_core's protocol-prefix match already catches -- so this exclusion is redundant with selection_core for this logsource, not a distinct signal being missed. Fires regardless of HTTP status, same reasoning as DETECT-2026-0037's traversal rule and stronger: the literal `${jndi:` syntax and its obfuscated forms are essentially never present in benign traffic (unlike a bare `../` or a SQL keyword), so status-gating would only cost recall against the exact behavior Masha's brief highlights -- mass scanners hitting paths that don't exist and getting a 404, or crashing app logging and getting a 500 -- without meaningfully improving precision.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: An authorized Nessus scan's own safe JNDI validation payload is filtered out by filter_nessus; a different scanner or a hand-rolled Log4Shell checker (nuclei, an internal canary script) that doesn't use Nessus's callback fingerprint still matches -- correlate with the scan calendar or source IP before escalating. Note that the same Nessus scan DOES alert in DETECT-2026-0038, which matches "Nessus" as a scanner User-Agent. The two rules handle it differently on purpose, not inconsistently: 0038 reports tool identity (an authorized scanner touching the host is still worth seeing in the activity feed), this rule reports an exploitation attempt, and a scanner's own safe validation probe is not one. Expect a 0038 hit with no 0043 hit for the same request.

Known blind spot: POST-body payloads (e.g. a JSON field carrying the lookup string) are invisible in the access log, same limitation as DETECT-2026-0041's SQLi rule. nginx logs the request line and headers raw/undecoded, so matching is literal -- but not case-sensitive: the `contains` modifier renders as a Splunk `search` field-value comparison, which is case-INsensitive (only `eval`/`where` comparisons are case-sensitive), so `${JNDI:LDAP:/` and `${Jndi:` casing variants of the listed strings are covered without separate entries. Same behaviour DETECT-2026-0037 relies on for its encoded traversal forms.

Known blind spot, second one: headers other than User-Agent and Referer are not in this repo's nginx log_format at all. X-Api-Version was one of the original 2021 delivery vectors (named in the description) and the 2021 wave also abused X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, Authorization, Cookie and arbitrary custom headers -- a payload delivered in any of those is invisible here, and no amount of pattern work in this rule can recover it. Closing that gap is an nginx log_format change, not a detection-logic change; noting it so the rule's coverage is not read as "all headers".

Alert volume, not false positives: the network-telescope research behind this rule found generic obfuscated JNDI probing is still constant background scanning years post-disclosure. Genuine application-level false positives on the literal `${jndi:` syntax and its listed obfuscations are effectively unheard of -- this is a high-specificity signal, unlike the ubiquitous-keyword problem SQLi/XSS rules have to gate around.
rules.rule_body:
detection:
  selection_sourcetype:
    sourcetype: access_combined
  selection_core:
  - useragent|contains:
    - ${jndi:ldap:/
    - ${jndi:rmi:/
    - ${jndi:ldaps:/

rules.title: Network Sniffing Tool and Windows Native Packet Capture Execution
rules.description:
Detects execution of network packet-capture tooling on a monitored Windows host, covering both third-party sniffers and Windows' own built-in capture facilities being invoked outside routine administration: Wireshark, tshark, dumpcap, and WinDump (all built on the Npcap/WinPcap capture driver); RawCap (a standalone sniffer that needs no driver at all, since it captures via raw sockets); the built-in `netsh trace start capture=yes` packet trace; the built-in `pktmon` packet monitor; and the PowerShell NetEventSession cmdlet sequence (New-NetEventSession / Add-NetEventPacketCaptureProvider / Start-NetEventSession) that drives the same underlying NDIS capture provider from a script.
This is process-creation telemetry only: it detects the tool or built-in utility being launched, not the on-wire sniffing itself, and it does not cover the Npcap/WinPcap driver *installation* step (a Sysmon EventID 6 DriverLoad for npcap.sys/npf.sys) or NIC promiscuous-mode changes -- this repo has no rule on any driver_load-category logsource yet, so that signal is a known coverage gap rather than something folded into this rule unverified.
rules.author: Bence Marton
falsepositives: Network engineers and helpdesk staff legitimately troubleshooting connectivity or VPN issues with Wireshark/tshark, `netsh trace`, or `pktmon` (`pktmon` is Microsoft's own documented tool for Always On VPN diagnostics) -- these are the most likely source of benign hits and the reason this rule is not rated critical. RawCap has essentially no such legitimate enterprise use (it exists specifically as a portable, no-install sniffer), so a RawCap hit should be treated with more suspicion than a Wireshark/pktmon/netsh hit even though they share this rule. The PowerShell NetEventSession branch also has genuine scripted diagnostic use, though it is rarer in practice than the GUI/CLI tools.
rules.rule_body:
detection:
  selection_capture_tools:
  - Image|endswith:
    - \tshark.exe
    - \dumpcap.exe
    - \windump.exe
    - \Wireshark.exe
    - \RawCap.exe
  - OriginalFileName:
    - tshark.exe
    - dumpcap.exe
    - WinDump.exe
    - Wireshark.exe
    - RawCap.exe
  selection_pktmon:
  - Image|endswith: \pktmon.exe
  - OriginalFileName: PktMon.exe
  selection_netsh_trace:
    Image|endswith: \netsh.exe
    CommandLine|contains|all:
    - trace
    - start
    - capture=yes
  selection_powershell_netevent:
    CommandLine|contains:
    - New-NetEventSession
    - Add-NetEventPacketCaptureProvider
    - Start-NetEventSession
  condition: selection_capture_tools or selection_pktmon or selection_netsh_trace or selection_powershell_netevent
